ok so hear me out. Everyone is asking WHO is transmitting on 2182 from a station that's been dead since 1987. I think I know.

"The light is out" is a CODE PHRASE. Four seven is a station number. Someone switched something back on.
Full writeup on my page: /~junebug/lantern.html

Older. That's a Coast Guard communications drill, the way they ran
them in the late seventies: station name three times, the drill
phrase, then the drill number. "Four seven" would be drill 47.
Nobody has run a drill like that on 2182 since the stations
were consolidated.

had a tape of them. I said in September it stank. I'm sorry I
was right.

artifacts.title: Mains hum: the fingerprint of the wall socket
artifacts.author: dotmatrix
artifacts.raw:
Mains hum: the fingerprint of the wall socket

Anything plugged into the wall in North America leaks a little 60 Hz into the recording, plus its harmonics at 120, 180 and 240 Hz. In Europe it's 50 Hz. You can't hear it most of the time. A spectrogram shows it as thin, perfectly straight lines.

Two things follow:

  1. If a recording claims to come from a battery radio in a field, it should not have 60 Hz lines in it.
  2. If the hum appears in one part of a recording and not in another, those parts were probably not recorded on the same machine at the same time. That's a splice.

Reel-to-reel decks also leave a slow wobble ("wow") around 0.5 Hz from the capstan. Cassette wobble is faster. Tape has a fingerprint too.

Plan:
10/20/99

The move failed. My fault, nobody else's.

Saturday night 1am I ran the full backup to DAT like I planned in August.
I did not verify the tape. I piped tar's output to a file and went to bed.
Sunday morning I shut beacon down, pulled the old drive, and ran mke2fs
on it so I could reuse it in the new box for swap. Then I drove to Seattle.

On the new box, the restore died at 38%. Read errors on the tape past
block 41,000-something. The tape drive had been throwing write errors
all night. It's in the log file I never read.

So: what's on the new server is whatever came off the first 38% of the
tape. The forum database is in pieces. Most of the homepages are gone.
The old disk is wiped.

I put a placeholder page up so people know we're not dead.
I'm so sorry, everyone. Ten years of doing backups for a living.
-r

artifacts.title: About the Lighthouse Network
artifacts.author: keeper
artifacts.raw:
About us

The Lighthouse Network was started by Mara Quinlan on March 14, 1997, as a single page on a free host with a guestbook and a list of frequencies.

My grandfather kept the light at Heceta Head for eleven years. He used to say a lighthouse is just a radio that speaks with its eyes. When the Coast Guard automated the lights, the keepers went home and the radio rooms went quiet. I wanted a place for the people who still listen.

In August 1997 Ray Tillman offered us a home on his own server, beacon, which lives in his garage in Tacoma and has been running ever since (mostly).

What we do

  • Keep the Log Book, a public database of everything our members have heard and recorded.
  • Visit decommissioned stations and photograph what is left.
  • Argue, politely, on the forum.

Who runs it

Mara Quinlan (keeper) — founder and administrator.
Ray Tillman (sysop_ray) — system administrator and owner of the server.

Only the two of us have administrator accounts.
